doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

chapter: Finding her voice as a composer
title: Bringing Japanese drums and bent notes into the big band
summary: The kotsuzumi, Noh, Kogun, and Mingus's bent notes.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: That’s fascinating, really. Was it a challenge then to, you started delving into oriental music and themes and so forth, to transfer that to this big band format?

Yes. I think that first of all — excuse me — I would like to think my big band is a real — it’s an extension of a small group, that’s the way I like to think. But there are many things that happen because of the first band, what they could do and so on and so on, I utilize them, blah blah blah blah. But when — as I say before — I decided at least I should try that. I was very fascinated by a Japanese drum called kotsuzumi, because my late father was a student of Noh, N-O-H, a man’s performing art, he was a student of Noh and it was very familiar to me, and this is primitive works but they have such a beautiful sound and two headed drums and a tight string and played like this, and another one played like that. This one is bigger, it makes a higher pitch. The one that’s smaller, this makes a lower sound pitch, a little more resonant, and you change with a squeezed string. Also you change the pitch with, there’s a certain Japanese paper. You keep putting in to the change pitch, you know the way you like. That’s what they do. But I was very fascinated with that, I always wanted to utilize that. So that was around “Kogun” was the first one, that was 1974. But I always think that it’s just enough to make it effective, but it’s not going to be a major takeover, something like Brazilian music that became sort of a major change in the jazz scene, like the things called samba jazz or what have you. And it would never become that way but it’s a little different. And also there are a few things when I was with Mingus, he used to bend the note, which is very much oriental. And I don’t think he did it purposely but when I was with his group we rehearsed without anything. He would sing and you would have to kind of imitate it. So he sang and then the saxophone player and trumpet player would have to imitate what he sings. I think

that’s the best way to learn music I think. So some of the music was like a little bended a certain way, and I think that’s also very common in Japanese music, many notes are bended. The artistry of the Japanese instrumental music, it’s another skill but to change the shape of one note. That’s the artistry, and that includes bending a note also, so on and so on. So I think it becomes more like a color, a little bit different I think.
